note:
Doomscroll interviews [Jennifer C. Pan].

* " ... That is ... why these boring universal social democratic reforms ... are much more important than anti-racism ... Black and brown people are disproportionality represented in the working class so any program that will help  ... "
* The great compression: 1940-1970 where the wealth disparity became much smaller (in the USA). Post 1970s, gains started being diverted to the top 1%

As far as I understand, [Pan] looks to be pointing out a few things:

* There's a voting block (maybe 20%) that is economically liberal but culturally conservative. As the democrats become more economically conservative but culturally liberal, this block moves away from the democrats, potentially going to republicans or independent
* "Bread and butter issues", nationalized/socialized/single player healthcare, wage security, education, food security, housing security, etc. not only would be politically favorable but would go a long way towards helping marginalized groups, much more than many of the DEI initiatives
* The DEI initiatives have a lot of money (~$3B-$15B) being given to them (compared to something like the National Labor Relations Board (NRLB) is funded at around $300M). Maybe there's not  a clear picture as to the benefit they provide but businesses keep providing these programs and spending money on them, despite political backlash. From the 1980s onward, businesses have been steadily investing in DEI (under different names, affirmative action, sensitivity training, etc.)
* Re: the racial wealth gap, [Matt Bruenig] has some articles on wealth, poverty, including analysis by race. [Pan] talks about how the bottom 50% of the population, regardless of race, have no wealth at all
* Re: anti-racism, which tries to talk about structural racism instead of focusing on interpersonal racism ... " ... I am somewhat sympathetic ... it feels like a way to move away from talking about what's in peoples minds and hearts and instead talking about material things (redistributing wealth, etc.) ... but ... when you ... fixate on these racial disparities ... you come to these wrong solutions ... like going down the road of ... 'we need to address historical racism or we need to do something special' instead of [implementing] these universal ... social democratic reforms "

Not [Pan] but [Citarella] talks about 2020 democratic candidates each had their own niche policies about reparations except for [Sanders] and each of the niche policies would result in less wealth redistribution the more universal policies of [Sanders].

[Pan]:

* "I think that corporations and a lot of politicians ... like the idea of reparations and race targeted measures because ... it actually costs less money in the long run than something that is a universal sweeping reform like Medicare for all. It sounds ... progressive ". [Pan] goes on to talk about how it's a form of means testing (making sure people fall below a certain measure of income ("means") before qualifying) and that makes them unpopular and fragile

Doomscroll videos from this time (2023-2025) have an intentional segment about the enlightenment and asking folks directly whether they're fan of the enlightenment, if the ideas should be discarded and whether it's inherently racist. I think this is a push back against some talking points at the time which I'm already forgetting (now in 2026).

[Pan]'s book (now released) is "Selling Social Justice: Why the Rich Love Antiracism".
